newsitem.title: USA: Warner Records cuts jobs amid industry woes.
newsitem.headline: Warner Records cuts jobs amid industry woes.

text.p: In another sign of sluggish music markets, Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Bros. Records said this weekend it is cutting the national staff of its black music division by 35 to 40 percent.

While the cutbacks amount to less than 20 people, they struck a sour chord in the music industry, coming just days after PolyGram NV announced on Wednesday it was laying off 400 people and taking a $90 million charge in 1996 to restructure its music operations.
The latest Warner cutbacks also come closely on the heels of more than 60 job cuts announced this month at Time Warner's Atlantic Group, which also dropped several bands and artists from its roster.
A Warner spokesman said the moves at the two sister labels, Warner Bros. and Atlantic, were unrelated to each other or to Time Warner's recently completed takeover of Turner Broadcasting System Inc.
Senior Vice President Denise Brown of Warner's black music division said, "We've adjusted our overhead to better reflect the marketplace and out current needs.
"At the same time, we're looking forward to maximizing our efforts in the black music area with our leaner and more competitive posture," she said.

Shakeouts are expected to continue in the music industry, which faces increasing difficulty and stagnant sales growth as many consumers have completed replacing their vinyl records with compact discs.

Industry sources also note that many distribution arms of the world's major record labels, including Seagram's MCA, Time Warner's Warner Bros., Sony's Sony Music, Polygram, Bertelsmann AG's BMG and EMI Plc are experiencing album returns amid sweeping record store closings and bankruptcies.

"The entertainment industry is volatile by nature, but the record industry is most volatile because of the short-lived nature of success," said Tess Taylor, president of Los Angeles Music Network, an association that promotes career advancement and education for record industry professionals.
"The amount of new releases is increasing dramatically with a frenzy among the labels to get product out there to compete," Taylor said.
Pricing and costly contracts have also pressured margins, industry sources note.

At recent record industry symposium, Tom Siverman, chairman of independent label Tommy Boy Music, cited statistics by Soundscan, which monitors record industry sales, and said that only 148, or about 0.5 percent, of the 26,000 albums released in 1995 sold more than 250,000 units.
"This is only the break-even point at most major record companies. Most artists rarely have success after eight years," said Silverman.
He added that it was misdirected to build the business around exceptions such as R.E.M.'s landmark $80 contract to Warner Bros. that was announced in August.
That deal was said to be the largest recording contract in history, eclipsing Janet Jackson's estimated $70 million contract with Virgin Records, signed last January.
Warner, which has been distracted by management restructuring over the past years, is said to have written several big checks to hold on to its most influential acts.
Its roster includes Eric Clapton, Green Day and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.
At the symposium, Silverman noted that R.E.M.'s latest record, "New Adventures in Hi-Fi," debuted at a disappointing Number 2 and dropped 55 percent in its first week on the charts.
"Ego is costing the industry millions of dollars a year," he said.
In coming weeks, record labels face further challenges in as they gear up with promotions and new releases in the Christmas quarter, which accounts for about 40 percent of sales.
